title: Multilingualism & Translanguaging

pts: Translanguaging describes how multilingual speakers draw fluidly on their entire linguistic repertoire as one integrated system, not two separate languages switched between.
This reframes a learner's L1 (and any other languages) as an integrated cognitive resource, not interference to be minimised.
This directly challenges long-standing English-only classroom orthodoxy in communicative methodology.

v: A short transcript of multilingual group talk

items: Read a transcript in which learners mix languages while solving a task.
Mark every ‘switch’ between named languages.
Now ask what each learner is doing at each moment: planning, checking, finding a word, joking.
Compare the two readings. Which tells you more about the learners’ thinking?
Discuss what a strict English-only rule would have prevented.
Record (with consent) two minutes of your own learners’ group work and analyse it the same way.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Class 9 learners in Mysuru planning a water-saving poster (written for this book):

lines: S1: We need three tips. First, turn off the tap when brushing.
S2: Haudu, and bakeṭ-alli wash the car, not pipe.
S1: Bucket, not hose pipe. Tip two: use a bucket to wash vehicles.
S3: What is maḷe nīru saṅgraha… rain water collecting?
T: Rainwater harvesting.
S3: Rainwater harvesting. Tip three.

blocks.x: Read as switching, S2 and S3 ‘fail’ to stay in English. Read as translanguaging, they use Kannada to generate and test ideas, then produce accurate English for the poster.

body: Purpose: to contrast the two models. Content: on the left, a speaker with two separate boxes (‘Kannada’, ‘English’) joined by a switch; on the right, the same speaker with one pool of overlapping coloured features. Style: clean diagram, labels as well as colours. Board version: two boxes versus one overlapping circle.

items: A phone’s voice recorder (free); transcribe multilingual stretches by hand, since automatic tools handle them poorly.

blocks.x: Note short exchanges on a clipboard as you move between groups.

pts: Strict English-only classroom policy emerged partly from audiolingual-era concerns about L1 interference now substantially revised by SLA research.
This connects to Unit 64's argument that strategic L1 use can serve learning rather than undermine it.
The revision doesn't argue for abandoning target-language exposure — it argues against treating any L1 presence as inherently harmful.

v: Eight statement cards about L1 use

items: Give pairs statement cards such as ‘Never allow the mother tongue; it causes interference’.
Pairs place each on a timeline: audiolingual era, early communicative teaching, recent research.
For each, name the theory of learning behind it.
Decide which you would still defend, and under what conditions.
Compare with your school’s written or unwritten policy.
DIET faculty can run this with trainee teachers, adding statements from trainees’ own schooling.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: ‘Every word of Hindi is a lost opportunity for English.’ Assumes learning depends only on exposure time.
‘Errors come from the mother tongue, so keep it out.’ Assumes transfer is always negative; it can help as well as hinder.
‘Use English as much as possible, and other languages when they help learning.’ Assumes both exposure and understanding matter.

blocks.x: Elsa Auerbach (1993) argued that English-only policies rested more on ideology than on evidence. As Unit 64 showed, the modern position keeps rich English exposure while rejecting the idea that any other language in the room is harmful.

body: Purpose: to show changing views of L1 use. Content: a pendulum swinging between ‘Translate everything’ and ‘Target language only’, coming to rest in a central zone labelled ‘Purposeful use’. Style: simple infographic with era labels. Board version: an arc with three labels.

items: Padlet (free plan, limited boards) for a shared digital timeline.

blocks.x: Statement cards pegged along a string in the staff room.

pts: Many language learners globally are already multilingual before beginning English study, not monolingual speakers of a single L1.
Pedagogy designed around an assumed monolingual L1 baseline can misfit this common, often more complex, linguistic reality.
This connects to Unit 24's intercultural competence work, extended to genuinely multilingual, not just multicultural, awareness.

v: Outline of a person on paper; coloured pens

items: Each learner colours an outline of a person to show their languages: where they feel each one and when they use it (a ‘language portrait’).
Beside it they write: I use… with… when…
Groups compare portraits and count their languages.
The class builds a tally on the board.
Older learners write a paragraph, ‘My languages’, for their portfolio (Unit 42).
Support: sentence frames and a word bank (grandmother, market, prayer, phone).
Challenge: learners note which language they think in for maths, jokes or dreams, and why.

blocks.x: A learner’s notes (written for this book):

lines: I speak Telugu with my grandmother and Kannada with my friends. I use Hindi for films and English in school and on my phone. I think in Telugu when I am angry!

blocks.x: Class tally for 8B (fictional, 48 learners): Hindi 44, Kannada 41, Urdu 12, Telugu 9, Tamil 6, Konkani 2, Lambani 1, English 48. The single ‘mother tongue’ box on a school form hides this complexity, as does any plan that assumes one L1, for example in contrastive pronunciation work (Unit 4). The map extends the intercultural work of Unit 24 to multilingual awareness.

body: Purpose: to show the multilingual self. Content: an outline figure with head, heart and hands coloured differently and labels (‘Telugu – heart’, ‘English – school’, ‘Hindi – films’). Style: warm, child-drawn look. Board version: an outline with arrows and labels.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for a printable portrait template.

blocks.x: A hand-drawn outline; pencil shading if colours are scarce.

pts: Structured translanguaging tasks — previewing content in L1 before an English lesson, allowing multilingual brainstorming before English production — use the repertoire purposefully.
This differs from simply permitting unstructured L1 use whenever convenient, which risks reducing target-language practice time without a clear pedagogical purpose.
This connects directly to Unit 64's mediation tasks as one concrete, structured translanguaging application.

v: A B1 text on a science topic; a short home-language summary

items: Learners discuss the topic in home-language groups for five minutes, guided by two questions.
They read the English text with a clear English task (Unit 3).
They brainstorm answers to a discussion question in any language, as keywords.
Groups plan and deliver their answer in English only, with vocabulary support.
Ask which home-language words helped.
English text first, home-language check of understanding second, English output last.
Support: an English language bank for the production stage.
Challenge: learners write a bilingual glossary for a younger class.

blocks.x: A plan for ‘How a solar cooker works’ (written for this book):

lines: Stage 1 (5 min, any language): Where have you seen cooking with the sun?
Stage 2 (15 min, English): read the text; label a diagram.
Stage 3 (5 min, any language): Would a solar cooker work in your village?
Stage 4 (15 min, English only): prepare a one-minute answer: ‘It would work because… However…’.

blocks.x: Home languages activate knowledge and support thinking; English is the language of the product. That planned division is what separates pedagogical translanguaging from drift. The mediation tasks of Unit 64 are another structured form.

body: Purpose: to show structured stages. Content: stepping stones labelled with the stages, ‘any language’ stones patterned, English stones solid, ending at a flag labelled ‘English product’. Style: clear, sequential. Board version: boxes marked ‘any’ or ‘EN’ with arrows.

items: Google Translate (free) to draft a quick summary, checked afterwards by a fluent colleague or learner.

blocks.x: Two learners summarize the topic orally for their groups.

body: Announce each stage’s languages aloud: ‘For five minutes use any language to think. After that, English only for the poster.’ Clear signals prevent drift and make the return to English easy.

pts: Allowing brief access to a fuller linguistic repertoire during complex cognitive tasks can reduce processing overload, especially for genuinely difficult content.
This connects to Unit 37's CLIL cognitive-demand discussion, where language and content difficulty can compound problematically.
The benefit is task-dependent — high cognitive-load content-integrated tasks benefit more than routine language-practice tasks.

v: A demanding CLIL text, e.g. on urban flooding

items: Choose content that is conceptually as well as linguistically hard (Unit 37).
Groups tackle a problem question, reasoning in any language for ten minutes.
They write their solution in English.
A second, easier question is done in English throughout.
Discuss with learners which question needed their other languages.
Compare the solutions of groups who reason in any language with those who reason in English only, as a small inquiry (Unit 67).
Support: a bilingual glossary of five key concepts.
Challenge: learners explain the concept in English to a younger class.

blocks.x: Question (written for this book): Why does Bengaluru flood in heavy rain although it has no big river?

lines: Thinking note: lakes gone → kere mēle building → rain water ellige hōgutte? → drains block
English answer: Many lakes have been built over, so rainwater has nowhere to go. Blocked drains make it worse.

blocks.x: Cognitive load theory (Sweller 1988) holds that working memory is limited. When a hard concept and a hard language must be processed together, the demands add up; reasoning briefly in a stronger language can free capacity for understanding. The benefit depends on the task. In a routine vocabulary drill, other languages add little and take time from English.

body: Purpose: to show compounding demands. Content: a learner carrying bags labelled ‘hard concept’ and ‘hard language’; in a second panel, a friend labelled ‘home language’ carries one bag briefly, then hands it back. Style: light cartoon. Board version: two stick figures and two boxes.

items: Google Docs (free) for shared group notes in any script.

blocks.x: A group sheet divided into ‘Thinking notes (any language)’ and ‘Our answer (English)’.

pts: Positioning multilingualism as a valuable resource, rather than a deficit or obstacle, supports the identity and motivational dimensions discussed in Units 22 and 59.
This validates learners' full linguistic identity rather than implicitly treating their non-English languages as something to set aside in the classroom.
This connects directly to critical language awareness (Unit 59) — whose linguistic resources are valued is itself an ideological question.

v: Paper; drawings or photos; a family interview

items: Learners interview a family member, in any language, about a festival, recipe or proverb.
They draft a short English text, including the original words with a gloss.
After peer feedback (Unit 43), they produce an illustrated final version.
Texts are bound into a class book and shared with families.
Produce a dual-language version with a family member’s help.
Support: a frame (In my family we… My grandmother says… This means…).
Challenge: compare one proverb across three languages.

lines: My grandmother says, ‘Hani hani kūḍidare haḷḷa, tene tene kūḍidare baḷḷa’. It is a Kannada proverb: ‘Drop by drop makes a stream; blade by blade makes a rope.’ In English people say, ‘Little drops of water make the mighty ocean.’ I like the Kannada one better because it has two pictures.

blocks.x: Cummins and Early (2011) call such products identity texts: work in which learners invest their identities and which reflects them back in a positive light. A learner who sees their home language valued is more likely to experience English as an addition, not a replacement (Units 22 and 47). Whose languages appear on the wall is also a question of critical language awareness (Unit 59).

body: Purpose: to show identity texts on display. Content: an open handmade book with an English text, a line in Tamil script with a gloss, and a drawing of a festival. Style: warm, handmade. Board version: not applicable.

items: Book Creator (free plan with a limited library) or Google Slides (free) for a digital class book.

blocks.x: A stapled class book kept in the reading corner.

body: Cummins’s interdependence hypothesis proposes a common underlying proficiency across languages. A child who has learned to summarize or argue in Kannada does not have to learn the concept again in English, only the English forms (Cummins 2007).

pts: Allow multilingual dictionaries and brief L1 discussion for genuinely complex conceptual content, especially in mixed-ability or lower-proficiency contexts.
Design occasional tasks explicitly drawing on learners' full linguistic repertoire — comparing idioms across languages, multilingual vocabulary mapping.
Communicate clearly to learners when and why L1 use serves a specific pedagogical purpose, distinguishing it from unstructured default use.

items: Present eight idioms with example sentences.
Mixed-language groups find the nearest home-language equivalents.
They classify each pair: same image, different image, or no equivalent.
Each group shares one surprising pair.
Learners use two idioms in personalized English sentences.
Build a multilingual vocabulary map for a topic, with English at the centre.
Support: provide the equivalents for matching.
Challenge: discuss why some images travel across languages and others do not.

lines: a piece of cake → Hindi bāeṁ hāth kā khel (a game of the left hand): different image.
to add fuel to the fire → Hindi āg meṁ ghī ḍālnā (to pour ghee on the fire): similar image.
T: Why ghee in Hindi and fuel in English?
S1: Because ghee is poured into the fire in pooja.

blocks.x: The rule, stated clearly: other languages help us notice and remember the English expression; the sentences we write are in English.

body: Purpose: to show cross-language comparison. Content: a bridge with English idioms on one bank and Hindi, Kannada and Tamil equivalents on the other; planks labelled ‘same image’, ‘different image’, ‘no equivalent’. Style: bright. Board version: a three-column table.

pts: Some institutional contexts mandate English-only policy regardless of individual teacher pedagogical preference — real constraints Unit 25's practicality parameter acknowledges directly.
Even within such constraints, small, structured translanguaging moments can often be introduced without violating the broader policy's intent.
This is a genuinely evolving area of pedagogy — apply Unit 25's principled eclecticism rather than an all-or-nothing adoption.

v: Your school’s language policy; one lesson plan

items: Write down your school’s language policy as stated and as practised.
Name its intent: usually, maximum English exposure and practice.
In one lesson, find a stage where a short, structured translanguaging moment would serve that intent.
Plan the signal, the time limit and the return to English.
Teach it, note the effect, and discuss it with a colleague or head teacher.
Present the trial and your notes at a staff meeting.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A teacher’s note (written for this book):

lines: Policy: English only in English periods. Moment: pairs check ‘decentralization’ in any language for two minutes, then explain it in English with a frame.
Result: 30 of 44 learners gave an English explanation, against about 12 in a similar lesson last week. Time lost to English: two minutes.

blocks.x: Kumaravadivelu’s practicality parameter (Unit 25) accepts that institutions set real limits. Principled eclecticism means neither ignoring the policy nor treating it as a ban on thinking. The field is still evolving, so small, planned trials with evidence are wiser than wholesale adoption. Unit 88 returns to research on bilingual cognition.

body: Purpose: to show small structured moments within a policy. Content: a wall labelled ‘English-only policy’ with a small framed window through which learners glimpse their languages; a clock beside it. Style: calm, balanced. Board version: a rectangle with a small window.

items: Google Keep (free) for quick lesson notes.

blocks.x: A journal page with two columns: ‘What I tried’ and ‘What happened’.

body: Plan one structured translanguaging moment this week, with a purpose, a time limit and a return to English. Count how many learners contribute in English afterwards, and compare with a similar lesson taught without it.

dek: Unit 71 of 100: recognising and using learners' full linguistic repertoire as a resource — a significant shift from English-only classroom orthodoxy.

aims.x: Most learners in Indian classrooms arrive already speaking two, three or more languages. A child in Bengaluru may speak Urdu at home, Kannada with neighbours, Hindi at the market and some English at school. This unit asks what happens when we treat that whole repertoire as a resource for learning English rather than something to leave at the classroom door. It introduces translanguaging as a theory and as structured classroom practice, and is honest about its limits.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain translanguaging and how it differs from code-switching;
explain where English-only policy came from and why it has been revised;
describe the real multilingual profile of a class;
design structured translanguaging tasks with a clear purpose and a clear return to English;
judge when other languages reduce cognitive load and when they merely reduce English practice;
use multilingual tasks to support learner identity and motivation;
introduce small translanguaging moments within an English-only policy.

why: Why this matters. Most language learners are multilingual, not monolingual-becoming-bilingual. Translanguaging pedagogy takes that reality seriously rather than treating it as an obstacle.

background.x: The term translanguaging began in Welsh bilingual education, where Cen Williams used the Welsh trawsieithu for lessons in which input came in one language and output in the other (Williams 1994). Ofelia García and Li Wei (2014) developed it into a wider theory. A multilingual speaker, they argue, does not own separate language boxes and switch between them, but has one integrated repertoire from which they select features to suit the situation. Code-switching describes talk from the outside; translanguaging describes the speaker’s practice from the inside.

This view challenges a long tradition. Jim Cummins (2007) calls it the ‘two solitudes’ assumption: that languages should be kept strictly apart, that instruction should be in the target language only, and that translation has no place. Robert Phillipson (1992) described a related ‘monolingual fallacy’. Vivian Cook (2001) argued that the first language is a legitimate classroom resource, and Graham Hall and Guy Cook’s (2012) review showed that teachers everywhere use learners’ own languages, often with a guilt the research does not justify.

In India, multilingualism is the norm. Rama Kant Agnihotri (2014) describes children’s multilinguality as a resource for learning, and Unit 64 showed how mediation tasks draw on it. The National Education Policy recommends the home language as medium of instruction wherever possible until at least Grade 5, together with bilingual approaches (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020, para. 4.11). NCF 2023 treats multilingualism as a resource and encourages teachers to use learners’ languages in class (NCERT 2023).

None of this means abandoning English. Learners need large amounts of English input and practice (Units 31 and 32). The question is how, when and why other languages appear. Jasone Cenoz and Durk Gorter (2021) use pedagogical translanguaging for planned, teacher-designed practices, as distinct from the spontaneous mixing of everyday multilingual talk. This unit concentrates on the planned kind.

items: Language profile. A class profile from language portraits, with two planning decisions it leads to.
Task design. A lesson plan marking each stage ‘any language’ or ‘English’, with its purpose.
Identity texts. A class book assessed in English for content, organization and accuracy.
Evidence note. A short report on one classroom trial, with before-and-after observations of English output.
What was the language policy where you learned English, and how did it make you feel?
Which of your learners’ languages do you not speak? How could you learn about them?
When does home-language use in your class serve learning, and when does it fill time?
Which topics are hard enough in content to justify multilingual thinking time?
Whose languages are visible on your classroom walls?
How would you explain your approach to a head teacher who insists on English only?

terms.def: Moving between two or more languages within a conversation or sentence; in a multilingual classroom it can be a resource for learning rather than a sign of weakness.

The amount of mental effort a task places on working memory, which has limited capacity (Sweller 1988); reducing unnecessary load, for example by giving instructions in a home language, frees attention for learning.
Cummins’s idea that knowledge and skills developed in one language are shared across languages, so literacy developed in a home language supports learning English.
A piece of work, written, spoken or multimodal, in which learners invest their identities and which reflects them back positively, often using home languages (Cummins and Early 2011).
An activity in which learners colour a body outline to show their languages and how they relate to them. It reveals the richness of learners’ linguistic repertoires (Busch 2012).
The whole set of languages, dialects, registers and styles that a person can draw on; a learner in Bengaluru may use Kannada, Tamil, Hindi and English for different purposes.
The assumption that English is best taught through English alone, with learners’ other languages excluded (Phillipson 1992); research now supports purposeful use of the home language.
Planned instructional strategies that deliberately draw on learners’ whole linguistic repertoire, for example discussing in Kannada before writing in English, to support learning and understanding.

Using one’s full linguistic repertoire, across named languages, to make meaning and learn (García and Li Wei 2014). In class, learners might discuss a text in Kannada or Hindi before writing in English.
